templates.label: Blank custom experiment
templates.title: My experiment
templates.note: Your own evidence: start from zero and record resolved outcomes.

assumptions: Each variant has a stable success probability while you experiment.
Trials are comparable: the same kind of unit, drawn from the same population and environment.
Every variant uses one common success definition, judged at a fixed horizon.
Every trial costs the same, so choosing one more trial of any variant is an equal decision.
Outcomes are recorded only once they are resolved; pending trials are not counted.

references.title: Russo, Van Roy, Kazerouni, Osband and Wen, A Tutorial on Thompson Sampling (2018)
Auer, Cesa-Bianchi and Fischer, Finite-time Analysis of the Multiarmed Bandit Problem, Machine Learning 47 (2002)
Banerjee, ORIE 6154 lecture notes on multi-armed bandits (UCB1 formula cross-check)

hours.label: Next week's hours
hours.note: Fictional example counts for illustration, not real data. Use Clear example to start your own plan.
assumptions: Each activity has a stable chance that one of its hour-blocks feels worthwhile, and next week resembles the weeks the blocks came from.
Blocks are comparable: one hour each, judged the same way soon after, whatever the activity.
Every hour is interchangeable: no deadlines, minimums, fixed commitments or diminishing returns within the week.
The plan explores as well as exploits: an activity with few blocks can get hours because it might be best.
next: After each planned block, mark it worthwhile or not, add it to that activity's counts and make next week's plan from the new evidence.
If what counts as worthwhile changes, start the counts again rather than adding to them.
Neither method says an activity is conclusively best; both trade a little expected value now for learning.
